question: Give an example of when active listening changed the outcome of a conversation or project.

raiseTranscript.text: I was pairing on a ticket to add a new API endpoint. The other engineer kept saying the schema looked fine but something felt off about the error handling. I asked what specifically was bothering them and they explained a past incident where missing retries caused downtime. I added the retry logic and we caught two edge cases in review.
What exactly did you ask next after they said it felt off?
I asked them to walk me through the last time a similar endpoint failed. They described the retry gap and I realized we needed to handle 5xx responses differently.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when active listening changed the outcome of a conversation or project.
Role: New grad on first team, paired on API endpoint
Action: Asked follow-up on 'felt off' comment, surfaced prior outage details
Outcome: Added retry logic, caught edge cases before merge
Quote: 'I asked them to walk me through the last time a similar endpoint failed.'
Follow-up: Asked what question they posed next; candidate described specific clarification on error handling.
junior.raiseFeedback: The candidate described listening to a teammate's vague concern about an API schema during pairing. After asking the teammate to recount a prior outage, they added retry logic for 5xx responses and caught two edge cases. This shows basic ownership of their own work and willingness to adjust based on input. At junior level the scope is appropriately individual and the change stayed local to the ticket. The story demonstrates coachability through a concrete follow-up question rather than just nodding. Biggest gap is that the example stays tactical and does not yet show how they would surface the learning to others.

lowerTranscript.text: Once my manager told me the requirements were unclear so I listened and then just did what they asked. It worked out okay.
What question did you ask to understand the unclear part?
I didn't really ask anything extra, I just made sure I heard the words and coded it.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of when active listening changed the outcome of a conversation or project.
Role: Junior dev on feature work
Action: 'Listened' by repeating back manager words without probing
Outcome: 'It worked out okay' with no concrete change described
Quote: 'I just made sure I heard the words and coded it.'
Follow-up: Asked for the clarifying question used; candidate had none.
junior.lowerFeedback: The candidate offered a story where they 'listened' to a manager's note that requirements were unclear but took no further action beyond repeating the words. No specific question was asked and no outcome change resulted. At junior level we still expect evidence that the candidate can adjust their own work after input. The absence of any follow-up question or resulting adjustment shows limited ownership. The example stays at the level of passive hearing rather than active listening that alters behavior.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams had conflicting SLAs for a shared service. I sat in the planning meeting and noticed one side kept repeating 'we need sub-100ms p99' while the other focused on throughput. I asked each side to give their top two failure scenarios. That revealed the throughput team actually cared more about tail latency under load, so we renegotiated the SLA around the 99.9th percentile instead.
How did you get the second team to surface their real constraint?
I asked them to describe the last time the service had impacted their customers and what metric they had to explain to leadership.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when active listening changed the outcome of a conversation or project.
Role: Senior on platform team, cross-team SLA negotiation
Action: Asked each side for top failure scenarios instead of debating numbers
Outcome: Shifted SLA to 99.9th percentile after discovering real tail-latency concern
Quote: 'I asked each side to give their top two failure scenarios.'
Follow-up: How second team revealed real constraint; candidate cited customer-impact story question.
senior.raiseFeedback: The candidate used active listening in a cross-team SLA discussion by asking both sides to describe specific failure scenarios rather than arguing metrics. This surfaced that the real need was 99.9th percentile tail latency, changing the agreed SLA. At senior level the story shows influence without authority across team boundaries and a measurable outcome. The follow-up question they asked was targeted and produced new information. The example stays grounded without claiming heroic credit. Biggest remaining gap is limited evidence of teaching the technique to others on their team.

lowerTranscript.text: I was in a meeting where two teams disagreed on priorities. I summarized what each said and we moved on. Later the project slipped but at least everyone felt heard.
What question did you ask to understand the root of the disagreement?
I just restated their positions so they knew I was listening.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of when active listening changed the outcome of a conversation or project.
Role: Senior in cross-team planning meeting
Action: Summarized positions without probing deeper
Outcome: 'We moved on' and project later slipped
Quote: 'I just restated their positions so they knew I was listening.'
Follow-up: Probing question asked; candidate had only restatement, no discovery.
senior.lowerFeedback: The candidate described summarizing two teams' positions in a planning meeting and claimed this constituted active listening. No clarifying question was asked and the project still slipped, showing no change in outcome. At senior level we expect cross-team influence and evidence that listening produced a different decision or scope. The story offers only passive restatement without any resulting adjustment. This lowers the bar on the Communication competency for the level.

raiseTranscript.text: My team was about to commit to a large migration that the eng leads had scoped. In the planning review I noticed one quiet engineer kept saying 'we did something similar before.' I asked them to tell the room what had gone wrong last time. They described a data-loss incident that the leads had not considered. We added a rollback plan and reduced the migration scope by two weeks.
How did you make sure the quiet engineer felt safe speaking up?
I explicitly said their past experience was valuable and asked them to share it before any decision was locked.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when active listening changed the outcome of a conversation or project.
Role: Engineering manager, migration planning review
Action: Drew out quiet engineer on prior data-loss incident
Outcome: Added rollback and cut scope by two weeks
Quote: 'I asked them to tell the room what had gone wrong last time.'
Follow-up: How safety was created; candidate cited explicit invitation before decision lock.
manager.raiseFeedback: The manager noticed a quiet engineer referencing prior work during a migration review and created space for them to describe a past data-loss incident. This led to adding a rollback plan and trimming two weeks of scope. At manager level the example shows developing the team by surfacing under-heard input and changing a team-level outcome. The action was deliberate and produced a concrete metric change. The story demonstrates leverage through the team rather than the manager's own technical fix. The main gap is that it does not yet address how the manager would handle repeated underperformance in listening skills across the broader org.

lowerTranscript.text: I run retros every sprint and let everyone talk. One time someone mentioned a risk so we noted it and kept going.
What did you do after the risk was mentioned?
I thanked them for raising it and moved to the next agenda item.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of when active listening changed the outcome of a conversation or project.
Role: Manager running team retro
Action: Thanked person for risk mention then moved on
Outcome: Risk noted but no change described
Quote: 'I thanked them for raising it and moved to the next agenda item.'
Follow-up: Action taken after mention; candidate had none beyond acknowledgment.
manager.lowerFeedback: The candidate described running retros and acknowledging a risk mention without any follow-up action or scope change. At manager level we look for evidence that the manager creates leverage by turning team input into different team outcomes. The story shows only surface acknowledgment with no resulting decision or plan adjustment. This lowers the bar because the listening did not produce measurable team-level impact.

raiseTranscript.text: We were deciding whether to sunset a product line that still had vocal internal champions. In the exec review I asked each leader to describe the last customer escalation they personally handled on that product. Two leaders described the same class of integration failure that was costing enterprise renewals. We shifted the decision from full sunset to a six-month carve-out that protected the top 12 accounts and freed 40 engineers.
How did you surface the renewal impact that was not in the original deck?
I asked each person to name the single customer story that kept them awake at night rather than asking for data first.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when active listening changed the outcome of a conversation or project.
Role: VP-level exec in product sunsetting decision
Action: Asked leaders for personal customer escalation stories
Outcome: Shifted from full sunset to 6-month carve-out protecting 12 accounts and freeing 40 engineers
Quote: 'I asked each leader to describe the last customer escalation they personally handled.'
Follow-up: How renewal impact surfaced; candidate cited shift from data to personal customer story prompt.
exec.raiseFeedback: The executive changed a product sunsetting decision by asking leaders to recount their own recent customer escalations instead of reviewing the prepared data deck. This revealed a shared integration failure pattern affecting enterprise renewals, resulting in a six-month carve-out that protected twelve accounts and freed forty engineers. At exec level the story shows strategic judgment under ambiguity and org-level leverage. The prompt used was simple yet produced information that altered a multi-quarter business outcome. The example stays focused on trade-offs rather than heroics. The primary gap is limited detail on how this listening practice was institutionalized for other exec reviews.

lowerTranscript.text: In a strategy offsite the team debated two options. I made sure everyone got airtime and then we voted. The decision stuck.
What question changed anyone's mind during the discussion?
I didn't ask new questions; I just ensured the agenda gave equal time.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of when active listening changed the outcome of a conversation or project.
Role: Exec in strategy offsite
Action: Gave equal airtime then called a vote
Outcome: 'The decision stuck' with no change attributed to listening
Quote: 'I didn't ask new questions; I just ensured the agenda gave equal time.'
Follow-up: Question that altered a position; candidate had none.
exec.lowerFeedback: The candidate described running a strategy offsite with equal airtime and a vote but could not point to any question or insight that changed a position or outcome. At exec level we expect listening to drive strategic trade-offs at org or business scale. The story offers only process facilitation without evidence of new information or altered direction. This lowers the bar on Communication for the executive level.
